## Proof

Define $Q(x) = xP(x) - 1$. Since $\deg P = 1996$, we have $\deg Q = 1997$.

For each $n = 1, 2, \ldots, 1997$:
$$Q(n) = n \cdot P(n) - 1 = n \cdot \frac{1}{n} - 1 = 0.$$

So $Q$ has roots $1, 2, \ldots, 1997$ (1997 roots, matching its degree), hence
$$Q(x) = c\,(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-1997)$$
for some constant $c$.

**Finding $c$.** Evaluate at $x = 0$:
$$Q(0) = 0 \cdot P(0) - 1 = -1,$$
$$Q(0) = c\,(-1)(-2)\cdots(-1997) = c\,(-1)^{1997}\cdot 1997! = -c\cdot 1997!.$$
Thus $-c\cdot 1997! = -1$, giving $c = \dfrac{1}{1997!}$.

**Evaluating $P(1998)$.** 
$$Q(1998) = 1998\cdot P(1998) - 1,$$
$$Q(1998) = c\,(1997)(1996)\cdots(1) = c\cdot 1997! = \frac{1}{1997!}\cdot 1997! = 1.$$

Therefore
$$1998\cdot P(1998) - 1 = 1 \implies 1998\cdot P(1998) = 2 \implies P(1998) = \frac{2}{1998} = \frac{1}{999}.$$

$$\boxed{P(1998) = \dfrac{1}{999}}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
thinking:
The problem: P(x) degree 1996, P(n) = 1/n for n=1..1997. Find P(1998).

Standard approach: Let Q(x) = xP(x) - 1. Q has degree 1997. Q(n) = n·(1/n) - 1 = 0 for n=1..1997. So Q(x) = c·(x-1)(x-2)...(x-1997) for some constant c.

Leading coefficient of Q: xP(x) has leading coefficient = leading coeff of P, call it a. So Q leading coeff is a. The product (x-1)...(x-1997) has leading coeff 1, so c = a.

Now find a. Use Q(0) = 0·P(0) - 1 = -1. Also Q(0) = c·(0-1)(0-2)...(0-1997) = c·(-1)^{1997}·1997! = -c·1997!

So -c·1997! = -1, thus c = 1/1997!.

Now P(1998): Q(1998) = 1998·P(1998) - 1 = c·(1998-1)(1998-2)...(1998-1997) = c·1997·1996·...·1 = c·1997!

So 1998·P(1998) - 1 = (1/1997!)·1997! = 1.

Thus 1998·P(1998) = 2, P(1998) = 2/1998 = 1/999.
